q:
Five friends P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row, all facing north. P sits at the left end. R sits exactly in the middle of the row. T sits immediately to the left of R. Q sits somewhere to the right of S.
Who sits at the right end of the row?
solution:
Seats 1–5 from left to right (facing north, left = west).
P = 1, R = 3, T = 2 (immediately left of R).
S and Q take seats 4 and 5; Q is to the right of S ⇒ S = 4, Q = 5.
Row: P T R S Q, so Q is at the right end.
Trap: reading "Q to the right of S" as "S to the right of Q" gives S.

q:
Six people A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a straight row, all facing south.
• C sits at the extreme right end of the row.
• D sits second to the left of C.
• A sits immediately to the right of E.
• F does not sit next to D.
Who sits immediately to the left of D?
solution:
Number the seats 1–6 from west to east. Facing south, a person's right is west and left is east.
C is at the right end ⇒ C = 1. D is second to the left of C ⇒ D = 3.
F is not next to D ⇒ F ∈ {5, 6}. A is immediately right of E ⇒ A = E − 1, with (E, A) ∈ {(5, 4), (6, 5)}.
(E, A) = (6, 5) leaves no seat for F, so E = 5, A = 4, F = 6, B = 2.
Row (west→east): C B D A E F. Left of D (east side) is seat 4 = A.
Trap: using the "facing north" convention gives B.
verify:
OPTS = ["B", "A", "E", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDEF'):
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}          # 0 = west end
    right = lambda x, k=1: s[x] - k              # facing south: right is west
    left = lambda x, k=1: s[x] + k
    if s['C'] != 0: continue                      # extreme right end = west end
    if s['D'] != left('C', 2): continue
    if s['A'] != right('E'): continue
    if abs(s['F'] - s['D']) == 1: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[p.index('D') + 1])]

q:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, facing the centre. B sits second to the left of A. C sits opposite A. D sits immediately to the right of A. E is not a neighbour of C.
Who sits immediately to the left of C?
solution:
Facing the centre, left = clockwise. Number seats 0–5 clockwise with A = 0.
B = 2 (second to the left), C = 3 (opposite), D = 5 (right = anticlockwise).
Seats 1 and 4 remain; seat 4 is next to C, so E = 1 and F = 4.
Left of C (seat 3) is seat 4 = F.
Trap: B is the person to C's right.
verify:
OPTS = ["B", "E", "D", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('BCDEF'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 6
    if s['B'] == L('A', 2) and s['C'] == 3 and s['D'] == L('A', -1) and (s['E'] - s['C']) % 6 not in (1, 5):
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[(p.index('C') + 1) % 6])]

q:
Six persons P, Q, R, S, T and U sit around a circular table, all facing away from the centre. Q sits immediately to the right of P. R sits second to the left of P. S sits opposite P. T is not a neighbour of Q.
Who sits immediately to the left of S?
solution:
Facing outward, right = clockwise and left = anticlockwise. Seats 0–5 clockwise, P = 0.
Q = 1 (right of P), R = 4 (second to the left), S = 3 (opposite).
Seats 2 and 5 remain; seat 2 is next to Q, so T = 5 and U = 2.
Left of S = anticlockwise from seat 3 = seat 2 = U.
Trap: using the facing-centre rule gives R.
verify:
OPTS = ["R", "U", "T", "Q"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('QRSTU'):
    p = ('P',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    R = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 6   # outward: right = clockwise
    Lf = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] - k) % 6
    if s['Q'] == R('P') and s['R'] == Lf('P', 2) and s['S'] == 3 and (s['T'] - s['Q']) % 6 not in (1, 5):
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[(p.index('S') - 1) % 6])]

q:
In a row of students facing the teacher, Ravi is 11th from the left end and Meera is 17th from the right end. Ravi is to the left of Meera and there are exactly 4 students between them.
The total number of students in the row is ______.
solution:
Meera's position from the left = 11 + 4 + 1 = 16.
Total = (position from left) + (position from right) − 1 = 16 + 17 − 1 = 32.
Trap: forgetting the −1 gives 33; forgetting Meera herself gives 31.
verify:
cands = []
for N in range(1, 100):
    ravi, meera = 11, N - 17 + 1
    if meera - ravi - 1 == 4:
        cands.append(N)
assert len(cands) == 1
ans = cands[0]

q:
Seven students J, K, L, M, N, O and P scored different marks in a test. M scored the lowest. J scored less than only O. K scored more than L but less than N. P scored more than N.
How many students scored more than K?
solution:
"J scored less than only O" ⇒ O is 1st and J is 2nd.
M is 7th. Ranks 3–6 go to P, N, K, L with P > N > K > L ⇒ P 3rd, N 4th, K 5th, L 6th.
Students above K: O, J, P, N = 4.
verify:
OPTS = ["2", "3", "4", "5"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('JKLMNOP'):          # p[0] = highest score
    r = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if r['M'] == 6 and r['O'] == 0 and r['J'] == 1 and r['N'] < r['K'] < r['L'] and r['P'] < r['N']:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = sols[0].index('K')

q:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor. The floors are numbered 1 (lowest) to 6 (top).
• C lives on the top floor.
• A lives on the floor immediately above F.
• There are exactly two floors between the floors of B and A.
• E lives on a floor below B.
• D and F both live on odd-numbered floors.
Who lives on floor 4?
solution:
C = 6. F is on an odd floor and A = F + 1 ⇒ (F, A) ∈ {(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)}; (5, 6) is out since C = 6.
Two floors between B and A ⇒ B = A ± 3.
(F, A) = (3, 4): B = 1 (B = 7 impossible), but then E cannot be below B ✗.
(F, A) = (1, 2): B = 5. Floors 3 and 4 remain for D and E; D is odd ⇒ D = 3, E = 4 (below B ✓).
Floors 1–6: F, A, D, E, B, C.
verify:
OPTS = ["D", "B", "A", "E"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDEF'):           # p[i] lives on floor i+1
    f = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if f['C'] == 6 and f['A'] == f['F'] + 1 and abs(f['B'] - f['A']) == 3 and f['E'] < f['B'] and f['D'] % 2 == 1 and f['F'] % 2 == 1:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][3])]

q:
Five guest lectures P, Q, R, S and T are scheduled one per day from Monday to Friday of the same week. P is scheduled on the day after T. R is scheduled later in the week than P. S is scheduled before Q, and Q is not on Monday. There are exactly two lectures scheduled between Q and R.
Which lecture is scheduled on Wednesday?
solution:
Days 1–5 (Mon–Fri). T, P consecutive with R later ⇒ R ≥ 3.
Two lectures between Q and R ⇒ |Q − R| = 3 ⇒ (Q, R) ∈ {(1, 4), (2, 5), (4, 1), (5, 2)}. Q ≠ 1 and R ≥ 3 ⇒ (Q, R) = (2, 5).
S before Q ⇒ S = 1. Then T, P take 3, 4.
Order: S, Q, T, P, R.
verify:
OPTS = ["P", "T", "Q", "R"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('PQRST'):            # p[0] = Monday
    d = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if d['P'] == d['T'] + 1 and d['R'] > d['P'] and d['S'] < d['Q'] and d['Q'] != 0 and abs(d['Q'] - d['R']) == 3:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][2])]

q:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P sit in a row, all facing north.
• L sits third from the left end.
• Exactly two persons sit between L and O.
• N sits immediately to the right of K.
• M and P occupy the two ends of the row.
• P is not a neighbour of O.
Who sits exactly in the middle of the row?
solution:
Seats 1–7 from the left. L = 3 ⇒ O = 6 (two persons between; O = 0 is impossible).
M, P take seats 1 and 7. P is not next to O (seat 6) ⇒ P = 1, M = 7.
Seats 2, 4, 5 remain for J, K, N with N immediately right of K ⇒ K = 4, N = 5, J = 2.
Row: P J L K N O M; the middle seat 4 is K.

q:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E sit in a row that runs from west to east. Some of them face north and the others face south.
• A sits second to the right of C.
• B faces south and sits immediately to the left of A.
• D sits at one end of the row and faces the same direction as C.
• E sits immediately to the right of D.
• E faces the direction opposite to that of A.
• Exactly two of the five face south.
Who sits in the middle of the row, and which way does that person face?
solution:
Facing north, right = east; facing south, right = west.
Without the last two clues there are two rows: C facing south gives A B C E D (west→east) with A, B, C, D facing south; C facing north gives D E C B A with C, D facing north and B facing south.
In the first row A, B, C, D already face south — more than two ✗.
So the row is D E C B A with D, C, A facing north (A opposite to E ⇒ E faces south) and B, E facing south: exactly two ✓.
Middle seat: C, facing north.
Trap: stopping before the "exactly two face south" clue leaves C facing south as a possible answer.
verify:
OPTS = ["C, facing south", "B, facing south", "C, facing north", "E, facing north"]
from itertools import permutations, product
res = set()
for p in permutations('ABCDE'):
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}           # 0 = west
    for fs in product([1, -1], repeat=5):          # +1 north (right = east), -1 south
        f = dict(zip('ABCDE', fs))
        R = lambda x, k=1: s[x] + f[x] * k
        Lf = lambda x, k=1: s[x] - f[x] * k
        if s['A'] != R('C', 2): continue
        if not (f['B'] == -1 and s['B'] == Lf('A')): continue
        if not (s['D'] in (0, 4) and f['D'] == f['C']): continue
        if s['E'] != R('D'): continue
        if f['E'] != -f['A']: continue
        if list(fs).count(-1) != 2: continue
        mid = p[2]
        res.add(mid + (', facing north' if f[mid] == 1 else ', facing south'))
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res.pop())]

q:
Eight friends A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, facing the centre.
• A sits third to the left of E.
• B sits opposite E.
• C sits immediately to the left of B.
• D is a neighbour of A.
• F sits second to the left of G.
Who sits opposite D?
solution:
Facing the centre, left = clockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise with E = 0.
A = 3, B = 4 (opposite E), C = 5 (left of B).
D is next to A and seat 4 is taken ⇒ D = 2.
Seats 1, 6, 7 remain. F = G + 2: G = 7 gives F = 1 ✓; G = 6 gives F = 0 ✗ (E); G = 1 gives F = 3 ✗. So G = 7, F = 1, H = 6.
Opposite D (seat 2) is seat 6 = H.
verify:
OPTS = ["G", "C", "H", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDFGH'):
    p = ('E',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 8
    if s['A'] == L('E', 3) and s['B'] == 4 and s['C'] == L('B') and (s['D'] - s['A']) % 8 in (1, 7) and s['F'] == L('G', 2):
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[(p.index('D') + 4) % 8])]

q:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U sit around a circular table. Some of them face the centre and the others face away from the centre.
• P faces the centre, and Q sits second to the left of P.
• R sits opposite Q and faces away from the centre.
• S sits immediately to the left of R, and T sits immediately to the right of S.
• U faces the same direction as R.
Who sits immediately to the right of U?
solution:
Seats 0–5 clockwise, P = 0. For a person facing the centre left = clockwise; for one facing outward left = anticlockwise.
Q = 2; R = 5 (opposite), facing outward, so the left of R is seat 4 ⇒ S = 4.
If S faced outward, the right of S would be seat 5 (R) — so S faces the centre and T = 3. Then U = 1.
U faces outward (like R) ⇒ right of U = clockwise = seat 2 = Q.
Trap: assuming U faces the centre gives P.
verify:
OPTS = ["P", "T", "Q", "S"]
from itertools import permutations, product
res = set()
for p in permutations('QRSTU'):
    p = ('P',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    for fs in product([1, -1], repeat=6):          # +1 faces centre (left = clockwise)
        f = dict(zip(p, fs))
        L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + f[x] * k) % 6
        R = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] - f[x] * k) % 6
        if f['P'] != 1 or s['Q'] != L('P', 2): continue
        if (s['R'] - s['Q']) % 6 != 3 or f['R'] != -1: continue
        if s['S'] != L('R') or s['T'] != R('S'): continue
        if f['U'] != f['R']: continue
        res.add(p[R('U')])
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res.pop())]

q:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F have different heights. A is taller than B but shorter than C. D is shorter than B. E is taller than D. F is shorter than C but taller than A.
Which of the following persons could be the third tallest?
solution:
The chain is C > F > A > B > D; E is known only to be taller than D, so E can be anywhere above D.
E 1st or 2nd: third tallest is F. E 3rd: third tallest is E. E 4th or 5th: C F A … ⇒ third tallest is A.
B always has C, F, A above him, so B is at best 4th.
Possible: A, E, F.
verify:
OPTS = ["A", "B", "E", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
third = set()
for p in permutations('ABCDEF'):           # p[0] tallest
    h = {c: -i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if h['C'] > h['A'] > h['B'] and h['D'] < h['B'] and h['E'] > h['D'] and h['C'] > h['F'] > h['A']:
        third.add(p[2])
ans = sorted('ABCD'[OPTS.index(x)] for x in third if x in OPTS)
assert third <= set(OPTS)

q:
Five persons P, Q, R, S and T live on the five floors of a building (floor 1 is the lowest), one person per floor. Each likes a different fruit among apple, banana, cherry, grape and mango.
• P lives on the floor immediately below S.
• The person who likes mango lives on floor 3.
• Q lives on a floor above the person who likes cherry.
• The person who likes apple lives on the floor immediately above the person who likes grape.
• S likes cherry, and T does not like grape.
• The person who likes banana lives above the person who likes apple.
Which fruit does T like?
solution:
Mango is on floor 3, so the apple–grape pair is (2 above 1) or (5 above 4); banana is above apple ⇒ apple = 2, grape = 1.
Banana and cherry take floors 4 and 5; Q is above the cherry lover ⇒ cherry = 4, banana = 5 and Q = 5.
S likes cherry ⇒ S = 4, so P = 3 (mango).
R and T take floors 1 and 2; T does not like grape (floor 1) ⇒ T = 2: T likes apple (R = 1, grape).

q:
Five lectures P, Q, R, S and T are to be scheduled one per day from Monday to Friday. R must be on Wednesday. S must not be on Monday or Friday. T must not be on a day adjacent to R's day. P must be scheduled on an earlier day than Q.
The number of different schedules that satisfy all the conditions is ______.
solution:
R = Wednesday. S ∈ {Tue, Thu} (2 ways).
T is not adjacent to Wednesday ⇒ T ∈ {Mon, Fri} (2 ways).
The two days left go to P and Q with P first: 1 way.
Total = 2 × 2 × 1 = 4.
Trap: ignoring "P before Q" doubles the count to 8.

q:
Six persons U, V, W, X, Y and Z sit in a row, all facing north.
• V and W sit next to each other.
• X sits immediately to the right of Z.
• U sits at one of the two ends.
• Y does not sit next to U.
• W sits somewhere to the right of X.
Which one of the following statements is necessarily false?
options: Y sits at one of the ends.
U sits at the right end.
Z sits third from the left end.
V and Y sit next to each other.
solution:
The block Z X must have the block V W somewhere to its right, so Z X is near the left.
Listing all valid rows: UZXVWY, UZXWVY, UZXYVW, UZXYWV, YZXVWU, YZXWVU, ZXYVWU, ZXYWVU (8 rows).
Z is always in seat 1 or 2, never in seat 3 ⇒ the third statement is false in every row.
Y at an end (YZX…), U at the right end (…U) and V next to Y (UZXWVY) each happen in some row, so they are not necessarily false.

q:
Seven boxes J, K, L, M, N, O and P are stacked one above another in a single pile.
• Exactly three boxes are between K and N.
• L is immediately below K.
• M is somewhere above K.
• J is the fourth box from the top.
• P is either at the top or at the bottom of the pile.
• N is below O.
Which box is immediately above P?
solution:
Positions 1 (top) to 7 (bottom); J = 4. L = K + 1 and |K − N| = 4.
Possible (K, L, N): (1, 2, 5) ✗ (M must be above K); (2, 3, 6); (3, 4, 7) ✗ (J = 4); (5, 6, 1); (6, 7, 2).
N below O rules out N = 1; (6, 7, 2) needs O = 1 and then P has no end ✗.
So K = 2, L = 3, N = 6; M above K ⇒ M = 1; P takes an end ⇒ P = 7, O = 5.
Pile (top→bottom): M K L J O N P. Above P is N.
verify:
OPTS = ["O", "N", "L", "J"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('JKLMNOP'):              # p[0] = top
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if abs(s['K'] - s['N']) == 4 and s['L'] == s['K'] + 1 and s['M'] < s['K'] and s['J'] == 3 and s['P'] in (0, 6) and s['N'] > s['O']:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[p.index('P') - 1])]

q:
Arun, Bina, Chetan and Deepa sit around a square table, one on each side, all facing the centre. Bina sits to the right of Arun. Chetan does not sit opposite Bina.
Who sits to the left of Deepa?
solution:
Facing the centre, left = clockwise. Sides 0–3 clockwise with Arun = 0.
Bina is to Arun's right (anticlockwise) ⇒ Bina = 3; opposite Bina is side 1.
Chetan is not opposite Bina ⇒ Chetan = 2, Deepa = 1.
Left of Deepa (side 1) = side 2 = Chetan.
Trap: swapping left/right gives Arun.

q:
In a queue, Asha is 9th from the front and Bala is 15th from the back. Exactly 4 persons stand between Asha and Bala.
What is the minimum possible number of persons in the queue?
solution:
Case 1: Bala behind Asha ⇒ Bala is 14th from the front ⇒ total = 14 + 15 − 1 = 28.
Case 2: Bala ahead of Asha ⇒ Bala is 4th from the front ⇒ total = 4 + 15 − 1 = 18 (Asha, 9th, fits since 9 ≤ 18).
Minimum = 18.
Trap: considering only the first case gives 28.
verify:
OPTS = ["18", "19", "23", "28"]
cands = []
for N in range(1, 100):
    a, b = 9, N - 15 + 1
    if 1 <= b <= N and a <= N and abs(a - b) - 1 == 4:
        cands.append(N)
ans = min(cands)

q:
In a row of students, Kiran is 12th from the left end and Pooja is 18th from the right end. When Kiran and Pooja interchange their positions, Kiran becomes 21st from the left end.
The number of students in the row is ______.
solution:
After the swap Kiran occupies Pooja's old seat, so Pooja's old seat is 21st from the left.
That seat is also 18th from the right ⇒ total = 21 + 18 − 1 = 38.
Trap: adding Kiran's old position (12) instead gives 29.
verify:
cands = [N for N in range(1, 100) if 12 <= N and N - 18 + 1 == 21]
assert len(cands) == 1
ans = cands[0]

q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E sit around a circular table, facing the centre. B sits immediately to the left of A. D sits second to the right of A. E is not a neighbour of B.
Who sits immediately to the right of D?
solution:
Facing the centre, left = clockwise. Seats 0–4 clockwise, A = 0.
B = 1; D = second to the right (anticlockwise) = seat 3.
Seats 2 and 4 remain; seat 2 is next to B ⇒ E = 4, C = 2.
Right of D (anticlockwise from seat 3) = seat 2 = C.
Trap: E is to D's left.
verify:
OPTS = ["E", "C", "B", "A"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('BCDE'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if s['B'] == 1 and s['D'] == (0 - 2) % 5 and (s['E'] - s['B']) % 5 not in (1, 4):
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[(p.index('D') - 1) % 5])]

q:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, facing the centre. B sits second to the left of A. C sits opposite B. D sits immediately to the right of C. E is not a neighbour of A.
Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: F sits between A and B.
C sits immediately to the left of A.
D sits immediately to the right of B.
solution:
Seats 0–5 clockwise (left = clockwise), A = 0.
B = 2, C = 5 (opposite B), D = 4 (right of C = anticlockwise).
Seats 1 and 3 remain; seat 1 is next to A ⇒ E = 3, F = 1.
Clockwise: A F B E D C. F is between A and B ✓; E (3) is opposite A ✓.
C is immediately to the right of A, not the left ✗; right of B is F, not D ✗.
verify:
OPTS = ["F sits between A and B.", "E sits opposite A.", "C sits immediately to the left of A.", "D sits immediately to the right of B."]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('BCDEF'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if s['B'] == 2 and (s['C'] - s['B']) % 6 == 3 and s['D'] == (s['C'] - 1) % 6 and (s['E'] - s['A']) % 6 not in (1, 5):
        sols.append(s)
assert len(sols) == 1
s = sols[0]
t = [ (s['F'] - s['A']) % 6 == 1 and (s['B'] - s['F']) % 6 == 1,
      (s['E'] - s['A']) % 6 == 3,
      s['C'] == (s['A'] + 1) % 6,
      s['D'] == (s['B'] - 1) % 6 ]
ans = [l for l, x in zip('ABCD', t) if x]

q:
Seven cars P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are parked in a row of slots numbered 1 to 7 from left to right.
• Exactly two cars are parked between R and U.
• Q is in an even-numbered slot and is next to R.
• T is parked immediately to the right of V.
• P is at one of the two ends.
• S is parked to the right of U, but not at an end.
• V is in one of the first three slots.
Which car is in slot 4?
solution:
Q is even and next to R, and U is three slots from R. Possible (R, Q, U): (1, 2, 4), (3, 2, 6), (3, 4, 6), (5, 4, 2), (5, 6, 2), (7, 6, 4).
U = 6 leaves S (right of U, not at an end) no slot ✗. In (1, 2, 4) and (5, 4, 2) the pair V, T with V ≤ 3 cannot fit ✗. In (5, 6, 2), V, T = 3, 4 and then P and S share slots 1 and 7, but S cannot be at an end ✗.
So R = 7, Q = 6, U = 4, S = 5, P = 1, V = 2, T = 3.
Row: P V T U S Q R ⇒ slot 4 is U.

q:
A building has four floors numbered 1 (lowest) to 4 (top). Each floor has two flats, an east flat and a west flat. Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H live in the eight flats, one in each.
• A lives in the west flat of an even-numbered floor.
• D lives in the flat immediately above A's flat.
• F lives on the same floor as A.
• B lives on the top floor, but not on the same side (east/west) as D.
• E lives in an east flat on a floor below F.
• C lives on the same floor as E, and H lives on the same floor as D.
Who lives in the flat immediately below B's flat?
solution:
D is directly above A, so A is not on floor 4 ⇒ A = floor 2 west, D = floor 3 west, F = floor 2 east.
B is on floor 4, not on D's (west) side ⇒ B = floor 4 east.
E is in an east flat below floor 2 ⇒ E = floor 1 east, so C = floor 1 west.
H is on floor 3 ⇒ H = floor 3 east; G = floor 4 west.
Directly below B (4 east) is 3 east = H.
Trap: D is below G, not below B.
verify:
OPTS = ["D", "H", "G", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDEFGH'):       # index = 2*(floor-1) + side, side 0 = west, 1 = east
    fl = {c: i // 2 + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    sd = {c: i % 2 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if not (fl['A'] % 2 == 0 and sd['A'] == 0): continue
    if not (sd['D'] == sd['A'] and fl['D'] == fl['A'] + 1): continue
    if fl['F'] != fl['A']: continue
    if not (fl['B'] == 4 and sd['B'] != sd['D']): continue
    if not (sd['E'] == 1 and fl['E'] < fl['F']): continue
    if fl['C'] != fl['E'] or fl['H'] != fl['D']: continue
    sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[p.index('B') - 2])]

q:
Five meetings P, Q, R, S and T are to be held on five of the six days from Monday to Saturday of a week, at most one meeting per day, so that exactly one of the six days has no meeting.
• The day with no meeting is the day immediately after R's meeting.
• Q is held two days after S.
• R is held before S.
• P is held after Q.
• T is not held on Monday.
Which meeting is held on Thursday?
solution:
Days 1–6 (Mon–Sat). Order so far: R, (free day), …, S, ·, Q, …, P with Q = S + 2 and P after Q.
R, the free day, S, Q and P need R + 1 < S, Q = S + 2 ≤ 5 ⇒ S ≤ 3 ⇒ R = 1, free day = 2, S = 3, Q = 5, P = 6.
The only day left is 4 (Thursday), which goes to T (and T is not on Monday ✓).
Thursday: T.
verify:
OPTS = ["T", "Q", "S", "P"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations(['P', 'Q', 'R', 'S', 'T', None]):   # p[0] = Monday
    d = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p) if c}
    free = p.index(None)
    if free == d['R'] + 1 and d['Q'] == d['S'] + 2 and d['R'] < d['S'] and d['P'] > d['Q'] and d['T'] != 0:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][3])]

q:
Five boxes P, Q, R, S and T have different weights. P is heavier than Q but lighter than R. S is lighter than Q. T is heavier than R.
Which box is the second heaviest?
solution:
Combine the facts into one chain: T > R > P > Q > S.
Second heaviest = R.
verify:
OPTS = ["P", "R", "T", "Q"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = [p for p in permutations('PQRST') if (lambda r: r['R'] < r['P'] < r['Q'] and r['S'] > r['Q'] and r['T'] < r['R'])({c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)})]
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][1])]

q:
Among five friends A, B, C, D and E, no two are of the same age. C is older than A but younger than E. B is younger than A. D is older than E.
If the five are lined up from the oldest to the youngest, who stands in the middle?
solution:
Chain: D > E > C > A > B.
The middle (3rd) position is C.
Trap: A is the "middle" of the first statement only.
verify:
OPTS = ["A", "E", "D", "C"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDE'):            # p[0] oldest
    r = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if r['E'] < r['C'] < r['A'] and r['B'] > r['A'] and r['D'] < r['E']:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][2])]

q:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit around a circular table, facing the centre. C sits third to the left of A. F sits immediately to the right of C. G sits second to the right of A. E sits immediately to the left of A. B is a neighbour of A.
Who sits third to the right of E?
solution:
Left = clockwise. Seats 0–6 clockwise with A = 0.
C = 3, F = 2 (right = anticlockwise), G = 5, E = 1.
B is next to A; seat 1 is E ⇒ B = 6, and D = 4.
Third to the right of E (anticlockwise from seat 1): seats 0, 6, 5 ⇒ G.
Trap: third to the left of E is D.
verify:
OPTS = ["D", "G", "C", "B"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('BCDEFG'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 7
    if s['C'] == L('A', 3) and s['F'] == L('C', -1) and s['G'] == L('A', -2) and s['E'] == L('A') and (s['B'] - s['A']) % 7 in (1, 6):
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
p = sols[0]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(p[(p.index('E') - 3) % 7])]

q:
Eight persons sit in two parallel rows of four seats each. P, Q, R and S sit in the north row facing south; A, B, C and D sit in the south row facing north, so that each person faces exactly one person of the other row.
• Q sits at an end of his row and faces B.
• R sits second to the right of Q.
• C faces S.
• A sits immediately to the left of D, and D does not sit at an end.
• P does not face A.
Who faces R?
solution:
Number seats 1–4 from west to east in both rows. North row faces south (right = west); south row faces north (left = west).
R is second to the right (west) of Q, so Q is at the east end: Q = 4, R = 2, and B = 4.
A is immediately west of D, D not at an end, seat 4 is B ⇒ (A, D) = (1, 2) or (2, 3).
(1, 2): C = 3 ⇒ S = 3, P = 1, but then P faces A ✗.
(2, 3): C = 1 ⇒ S = 1, P = 3 (faces D ✓).
R (seat 2) faces A.
verify:
OPTS = ["C", "D", "B", "A"]
from itertools import permutations
res = set()
for n in permutations('PQRS'):
    sn = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(n)}          # seat 1 = west
    for so in permutations('ABCD'):
        ss = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(so)}
        if sn['Q'] not in (1, 4) or ss['B'] != sn['Q']: continue
        if sn['R'] != sn['Q'] - 2: continue             # facing south: right = west
        if ss['C'] != sn['S']: continue
        if ss['A'] != ss['D'] - 1 or ss['D'] in (1, 4): continue   # facing north: left = west
        if ss['A'] == sn['P']: continue
        res.add(so[sn['R'] - 1])
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res.pop())]

q:
Thirty children sit in a row, all facing north. Hari is 9th from the left end and Gita is 8th from the right end.
How many children sit between Hari and Gita?
solution:
Gita's position from the left = 30 − 8 + 1 = 23.
Children between positions 9 and 23 = 23 − 9 − 1 = 13.
Trap: 23 − 9 = 14 counts one end; forgetting the +1 in the conversion gives 12.
verify:
OPTS = ["12", "13", "14", "15"]
N = 30
row = [None] * N
row[9 - 1] = 'H'
row[N - 8] = 'G'
i, j = row.index('H'), row.index('G')
ans = abs(i - j) - 1

q:
A building has seven floors numbered 1 (lowest) to 7 (top). Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F live in it, one on each of six floors; one floor is vacant.
• Nobody lives below D.
• A lives two floors above C.
• The vacant floor is somewhere above A.
• B and D live on adjacent floors.
• E and F both live on even-numbered floors, and E lives below F.
Who lives on floor 4?
solution:
D = 1, so B = 2. A = C + 2, with the vacant floor above A.
E and F take two even floors from {4, 6} (floor 2 is B) ⇒ E = 4, F = 6.
The remaining floors 3, 5, 7 hold C, A and the vacancy: C = 3, A = 5, vacant = 7 ✓.
Floor 4: E.
verify:
OPTS = ["A", "C", "E", "F"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('ABCDEF_'):
    f = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if f['D'] == 1 and f['A'] == f['C'] + 2 and f['_'] > f['A'] and abs(f['B'] - f['D']) == 1 \
       and f['E'] % 2 == 0 and f['F'] % 2 == 0 and f['E'] < f['F']:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][3])]

q:
Six seminars P, Q, R, S, T and U are held over Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, with one seminar in the morning slot and one in the afternoon slot of each day.
• R is held on Tuesday.
• Q is held in a morning slot, on the day after P's day.
• S and T are held on the same day, T before S.
• U is held in an afternoon slot.
• P is held in a morning slot.
• Q and U are held on the same day.
Which seminar is held on Monday afternoon?
solution:
S and T fill one whole day (T morning, S afternoon); R is on Tuesday, so S–T is on Monday or Wednesday.
Q (morning) and U (afternoon) are on the same day, so they fill another whole day; with R on Tuesday it must be Monday or Wednesday.
Q is the day after P ⇒ Q is not on Monday ⇒ Q, U on Wednesday; P is on Tuesday (morning) with R in the afternoon.
Monday: T (morning), S (afternoon).
verify:
OPTS = ["T", "U", "S", "R"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('PQRSTU'):          # slot index = 2*day + (0 morning, 1 afternoon)
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    d = {c: i // 2 for c, i in s.items()}; t = {c: i % 2 for c, i in s.items()}
    if d['R'] == 1 and t['Q'] == 0 and d['Q'] == d['P'] + 1 and d['S'] == d['T'] and s['T'] < s['S'] \
       and t['U'] == 1 and t['P'] == 0 and d['Q'] == d['U']:
        sols.append(p)
assert len(sols) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(sols[0][1])]

q:
Six students P, Q, R, S, T and U obtained different scores in a quiz. P scored more than Q. R scored less than S but more than P. T scored the least. U scored more than Q.
Which of the following statements must be true?
options: S is among the top two.
solution:
Chain: S > R > P > Q > T, and U > Q with U's place above Q otherwise free.
Possible orders: SRPUQT, SRUPQT, SURPQT, USRPQT.
Q is 5th in all ✓. S is 1st or 2nd in all ✓.
R is 3rd in SURPQT and USRPQT ✗; U is below P in SRPUQT ✗.
verify:
OPTS = ["Q ranks fifth.", "R ranks second.", "S is among the top two.", "U scored more than P."]
from itertools import permutations
rows = []
for p in permutations('PQRSTU'):           # p[0] = top
    r = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if r['P'] < r['Q'] and r['S'] < r['R'] < r['P'] and r['T'] == 6 and r['U'] < r['Q']:
        rows.append(r)
tests = [lambda r: r['Q'] == 5, lambda r: r['R'] == 2, lambda r: r['S'] <= 2, lambda r: r['U'] < r['P']]
ans = [l for l, f in zip('ABCD', tests) if all(f(r) for r in rows)]

q:
Five friends P, Q, R, S and T stand in a row for a photograph, all facing the camera. P does not stand next to Q. R stands at one of the ends. S stands immediately to the right of T. Q does not stand at an end.
Which one of the following could be the order of the five friends from left to right?
solution:
Check each option against the four conditions.
R T S Q P: Q is next to P ✗. P Q T S R: P next to Q ✗. Q T S P R: Q at an end ✗.
R Q T S P: R at an end ✓, S immediately right of T ✓, Q not at an end ✓, P (5th) not next to Q (2nd) ✓.

q:
Eight friends A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, facing the centre. D sits third to the right of A. B sits opposite D. G sits immediately to the left of D. C sits second to the left of B. F is not a neighbour of C. E is a neighbour of B.
Counting clockwise from E, how many persons sit between E and F?
solution:
Left = clockwise. Seats 0–7 clockwise, A = 0.
D = 5 (third to the right = anticlockwise), B = 1, G = 6, C = 3.
Seats 2, 4, 7 remain; F is not next to C (2, 4) ⇒ F = 7; E next to B ⇒ E = 2; H = 4.
Clockwise from E (2) to F (7): seats 3, 4, 5, 6 ⇒ 4 persons (C, H, D, G).
Trap: counting anticlockwise gives 2.
verify:
OPTS = ["2", "3", "4", "5"]
from itertools import permutations
sols = []
for p in permutations('BCDEFGH'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 8
    if s['D'] == L('A', -3) and (s['B'] - s['D']) % 8 == 4 and s['G'] == L('D') and s['C'] == L('B', 2) \
       and (s['F'] - s['C']) % 8 not in (1, 7) and (s['E'] - s['B']) % 8 in (1, 7):
        sols.append(s)
assert len(sols) == 1
s = sols[0]
ans = (s['F'] - s['E']) % 8 - 1

q:
Six runners A, B, C, D, E and F took part in a race; there were no ties. F finished ahead of C, C ahead of A, and A ahead of B. D finished immediately behind B. E was not last, and E finished behind A.
Who finished fourth?
solution:
Chain: F, C, A, B, D with D immediately after B.
E is behind A and not last; it cannot come between B and D ⇒ E is between A and B.
Order: F, C, A, E, B, D.

q:
Some children stand equally spaced around a circle and are numbered 1, 2, 3, … consecutively around it. Child number 7 is exactly opposite child number 22.
How many children are there in the circle?
solution:
Opposite children are half the circle apart: $22-7=15=\dfrac{n}{2}$.
So $n=$ 30.
Trap: 22 + 7 − 1 = 28 treats it like a row.
verify:
OPTS = ["28", "29", "30", "32"]
cands = [n for n in range(23, 100) if n % 2 == 0 and (22 - 7) % n == n // 2]
assert len(cands) == 1
ans = cands[0]

q:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F sit in six seats numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. A and B sit in the two end seats. C's seat number is twice D's seat number. E sits immediately to the right of C.
The seat number of F is ______.
solution:
Seats 1 and 6 are A and B, so C, D ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}.
C = 2D: (D, C) = (2, 4) is the only pair inside {2, …, 5}.
E = C + 1 = 5. The remaining seat is 3 for F (whichever end A and B take).

q:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table facing the centre. They are a doctor, an engineer, a lawyer, a pilot, a singer and a teacher, one profession each.
• C sits immediately to the left of A, and D is a neighbour of A.
• E sits second to the right of F.
• The doctor sits opposite B.
• The engineer sits immediately to the right of the doctor.
• The pilot sits opposite the singer, and F is not the pilot.
• The teacher sits immediately to the left of the pilot.
What is the profession of the person who sits opposite E?
solution:
Left = clockwise; seats 0–5 clockwise with A = 0. C = 1, so D = 5.
E is second to the right (anticlockwise) of F within seats 2–4 ⇒ F = 4, E = 2, B = 3.
Doctor opposite B ⇒ A is the doctor; engineer on A's right ⇒ D (seat 5).
Among C, E, B, F the only opposite pair is C–F ⇒ {pilot, singer} = {C, F}; F is not the pilot ⇒ C pilot, F singer.
Teacher is left of C ⇒ E; B is the lawyer.
Opposite E (seat 2) is D, the engineer.
verify:
OPTS = ["Singer", "Lawyer", "Pilot", "Engineer"]
from itertools import permutations
prof = ['doctor', 'engineer', 'lawyer', 'pilot', 'singer', 'teacher']
res = set()
for p in permutations('BCDEF'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    L = lambda x, k=1: (s[x] + k) % 6
    if s['C'] != L('A') or (s['D'] - s['A']) % 6 not in (1, 5) or s['E'] != L('F', -2): continue
    for pr in permutations(prof):
        w = dict(zip(p, pr)); at = {v: s[k] for k, v in w.items()}
        if (at['doctor'] - s['B']) % 6 != 3: continue
        if at['engineer'] != (at['doctor'] - 1) % 6: continue
        if (at['pilot'] - at['singer']) % 6 != 3 or w['F'] == 'pilot': continue
        if at['teacher'] != (at['pilot'] + 1) % 6: continue
        res.add(w[p[(s['E'] + 3) % 6]])
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res.pop().capitalize())]

q:
Seven families A, B, C, D, E, F and G live in seven houses numbered 1 to 7 in a row, one family per house.
• C's house number is twice A's house number.
• E's house number is 3 more than C's.
• B lives in one of the two end houses, and D lives next to B.
• G lives in an odd-numbered house.
Who lives in house number 4?
solution:
E = C + 3 ≤ 7 ⇒ C ≤ 4 ⇒ (A, C, E) = (1, 2, 5) or (2, 4, 7).
(2, 4, 7): B must take house 1 and D house 2, but 2 is A ✗.
(1, 2, 5): B = 7, D = 6. Houses 3 and 4 remain; G is odd ⇒ G = 3, F = 4.
House 4: F.

q:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U have their birthdays in six different months from January to June of a year.
• P's birthday is in a month that has 31 days.
• T's birthday is in the month immediately after P's.
• S's birthday is in June.
• Q's birthday comes after T's.
• R's birthday comes before P's, but not in January.
Whose birthday is in January?
solution:
Months with 31 days among Jan–Jun: January, March, May.
P = May ⇒ T = June, but June is S ✗. P = January ⇒ nobody (R) can be before P ✗.
So P = March, T = April, Q = May (after T, June is taken), R = February (before March, not January), and U = January.

q:
Six persons A, B, C, D, E and F sit in a row, all facing north. C sits third from the left end. A and B occupy the two end seats. D sits immediately to the right of C. E does not sit next to A.
Which one of the following must be true?
options: E sits second from the left end.
F sits immediately to the right of A.
B sits at the right end, or E sits second from the left end.
solution:
C = 3, D = 4; seats 2 and 5 are left for E and F.
Case 1: A = 1, B = 6 ⇒ E ≠ 2 ⇒ E = 5, F = 2: A F C D E B.
Case 2: B = 1, A = 6 ⇒ E ≠ 5 ⇒ E = 2, F = 5: B E C D F A.
"B at the right end" holds in case 1 and "E second from the left" in case 2, so the "or" statement holds in both.
The first and fourth statements hold only in one case; F is right of A only in case 1.

q:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a circular table, facing the centre. C sits second to the left of A. D sits opposite E. B is not a neighbour of A. Now A and D exchange their seats.
Which one of the following must be true after the exchange?
options: A sits immediately to the left of D.
C sits between A and B.
A sits immediately to the left of D, or A sits immediately to the right of F.
E sits immediately to the right of D, or A sits opposite B.
solution:
Left = clockwise; seats 0–5 clockwise, A = 0, so C = 2. B is not next to A ⇒ B ∈ {3, 4}.
B = 4 leaves seats 1, 3, 5 with no opposite pair for D, E ✗. So B = 3; D, E take 1 and 4 (either way) and F = 5.
Case 1 (D = 1, E = 4) after the swap: D0 A1 C2 B3 E4 F5 — A is left of D ✓.
Case 2 (E = 1, D = 4) after the swap: D0 E1 C2 B3 A4 F5 — A is right of F ✓.
So the "or" statement in option C holds in both cases; A and B hold in case 1 only; D holds in neither.
verify:
OPTS = ["A sits immediately to the left of D.", "C sits between A and B.", "A sits immediately to the left of D, or A sits immediately to the right of F.", "E sits immediately to the right of D, or A sits opposite B."]
from itertools import permutations
cases = []
for p in permutations('BCDEF'):
    p = ('A',) + p
    s = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if s['C'] == (s['A'] + 2) % 6 and (s['D'] - s['E']) % 6 == 3 and (s['B'] - s['A']) % 6 not in (1, 5):
        s['A'], s['D'] = s['D'], s['A']
        cases.append(s)
left = lambda s, x: (s[x] + 1) % 6
right = lambda s, x: (s[x] - 1) % 6
tests = {
 OPTS[0]: lambda s: s['A'] == left(s, 'D'),
 OPTS[1]: lambda s: {s['A'], s['B']} == {(s['C'] + 1) % 6, (s['C'] - 1) % 6},
 OPTS[2]: lambda s: s['A'] == left(s, 'D') or s['A'] == right(s, 'F'),
 OPTS[3]: lambda s: s['E'] == right(s, 'D') or (s['A'] - s['B']) % 6 == 3,
}
must = [o for o in OPTS if all(tests[o](s) for s in cases)]
assert len(must) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(must[0])]

q: Five friends P, Q, R, S and T have different heights. P is taller than Q. R is taller than S but shorter than T. If it is also known that Q is shorter than T but taller than R, who is the third tallest?
solution:
Facts: P > Q, T > R > S, and T > Q > R.
So Q is below both P and T and above both R and S.
P and T take the top two places (in some order); Q is third, then R, S.
Trap: the order of P and T is not fixed, but that does not affect the 3rd place.
verify:
OPTS = ["T", "P", "Q", "R"]
from itertools import permutations
third = set()
for p in permutations('PQRST'):            # p[0] tallest
    r = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(p)}
    if r['P'] < r['Q'] and r['T'] < r['R'] < r['S'] and r['T'] < r['Q'] < r['R']:
        third.add(p[2])
assert len(third) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(third.pop())]

q:
Five persons A, B, C, D and E sit in five seats numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. A does not sit at an end. B sits immediately to the right of A. C does not sit next to B. D sits somewhere to the left of E.
In which of the following seats could C sit?
solution:
(A, B) ∈ {(2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)}.
(2, 3): C ∉ {2, 4} ⇒ C = 1 or 5 (e.g. C A B D E, D A B E C).
(3, 4): C ∉ {3, 5} ⇒ C = 1 or 2 (e.g. D C A B E).
(4, 5): C ≠ 4 ⇒ C ∈ {1, 2, 3} (e.g. D E C A B).
C can never be in seat 4 (it would be next to B in every case). Possible: 2, 3, 5 (and 1).

q:
On an island every person is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. A says, "At least one of us two is a knave." B says nothing.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: A is a knight and B is a knave.
A and B are both knights.
A and B are both knaves.
A is a knave and B is a knight.
solution:
If A were a knave, the statement "at least one of us is a knave" would be true — a knave cannot say something true ✗.
So A is a knight and the statement is true: someone is a knave, and it is not A ⇒ B is a knave.
verify:
OPTS = ["A is a knight and B is a knave.", "A and B are both knights.", "A and B are both knaves.", "A is a knave and B is a knight."]
from itertools import product
res = []
for a, b in product([True, False], repeat=2):      # True = knight
    stmt = (not a) or (not b)
    if stmt == a:
        res.append((a, b))
assert len(res) == 1
a, b = res[0]
txt = {(True, False): 'A is a knight and B is a knave.', (True, True): 'A and B are both knights.',
       (False, False): 'A and B are both knaves.', (False, True): 'A is a knave and B is a knight.'}[(a, b)]
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(txt)]

q:
On an island every person is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
P says, "Q is a knave."
Q says, "P and R are of the same type."
R says, "Q is a knight."
How many of P, Q and R are knights?
solution:
If P is a knave, Q is a knight; then P and R are of the same type, so R is a knave — but R's statement "Q is a knight" would then be true ✗.
So P is a knight and Q is a knave. Q's statement is false ⇒ R differs from P ⇒ R is a knave; R's statement "Q is a knight" is indeed false ✓.
Knights: only P ⇒ 1.
verify:
OPTS = ["1", "0", "2", "3"]
from itertools import product
res = set()
for p, q, r in product([True, False], repeat=3):
    if (not q) == p and (p == r) == q and q == r:
        res.add(p + q + r)
assert len(res) == 1
ans = res.pop()

q:
Exactly one of the four children A, B, C and D broke a window. When questioned:
A said, "B broke it."
B said, "D broke it."
C said, "I did not break it."
D said, "B is lying."
If exactly one of these four statements is true, who broke the window?
solution:
Test each culprit and count the true statements.
A: C's and D's statements are true (2) ✗. B: A's and C's are true ✗. D: B's and C's are true ✗.
C: A false, B false, C false, D ("B is lying") true — exactly one ✓.
verify:
OPTS = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
res = []
for X in 'ABCD':
    sB = X == 'D'
    st = [X == 'B', sB, X != 'C', not sB]
    if sum(st) == 1:
        res.append(X)
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res[0])]

q:
Exactly one of five friends P, Q, R, S and T ate the last piece of cake. They said:
P: "Q ate it."
Q: "P did not eat it."
R: "Either S or T ate it."
S: "I did not eat it."
T: "Either Q or R ate it."
If exactly one of the five is lying, which one of the following is correct?
options: R ate it; P is lying.
T ate it; P is lying.
Q ate it; P is lying.
Q ate it; R is lying.
solution:
R's and T's statements cannot both be true (they name disjoint pairs), so the liar is R or T and everyone else tells the truth.
P is truthful ⇒ Q ate it. Check: Q ✓ (P did not), R ✗ (lie), S ✓, T ✓ (Q ate it).
Exactly one liar (R) ✓. So Q ate it and R is lying.

q:
Among three persons A, B and C, one always tells the truth, one always lies, and one is unpredictable (sometimes tells the truth and sometimes lies). Each knows who is who.
A says, "C is the liar."
B says, "A is the truth-teller."
C says, "I am the unpredictable one."
Who is the liar?
solution:
If A is the liar: B's claim is false, so B is not the truth-teller; B is unpredictable and C is the truth-teller — but then C's claim "I am unpredictable" is false ✗.
If A is unpredictable: B's claim is false ⇒ B is the liar ⇒ C is the truth-teller, whose claim is again false ✗.
So A is the truth-teller ⇒ C is the liar (A's claim), B is unpredictable; C's claim is false, as a liar's must be ✓.
Liar: C.

q:
In a football league of 12 teams, every team plays every other team twice (once at home and once away).
The total number of matches played in the league is ______.
solution:
Each unordered pair of teams meets twice: $2\times\binom{12}{2}=2\times66=$ 132.
Equivalently, each of the 12 teams hosts the other 11: $12\times11=132$.
Trap: 66 counts each pair only once.
verify:
from itertools import permutations
ans = sum(1 for h, a in permutations(range(12), 2))   # ordered (home, away) pairs

q:
A badminton knock-out tournament has 37 players. In every match the loser is eliminated, and byes are given wherever needed. There are no draws.
How many matches are played in all to decide the champion?
solution:
Each match eliminates exactly one player. To leave one champion, 37 − 1 = 36 players must be eliminated ⇒ 36 matches, however the byes are arranged.
Trap: 32 uses the nearest power of 2.
verify:
OPTS = ["36", "18", "32", "37"]
n, matches = 37, 0
while n > 1:
    m = n // 2          # pair up as many as possible, the odd one gets a bye
    matches += m
    n -= m
ans = matches

q:
Twenty teams are divided into 4 groups of 5. In the group stage every team plays every other team of its own group once. The top two teams of each group then enter a knock-out stage (quarter-finals, semi-finals and a final), and the two losing semi-finalists also play a third-place match.
What is the total number of matches played?
solution:
Group stage: each group has $\binom52=10$ matches ⇒ 4 × 10 = 40.
Knock-out among 8 teams: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 matches; plus the third-place match = 8.
Total = 40 + 8 = 48.
Trap: 47 forgets the third-place match; 197 treats the group stage as one round robin of 20.
verify:
OPTS = ["47", "48", "55", "197"]
from itertools import combinations
group = 4 * len(list(combinations(range(5), 2)))
n, ko = 8, 0
while n > 1:
    ko += n // 2; n //= 2
ans = group + ko + 1

q:
Eight teams play a round-robin tournament in which every pair of teams meets exactly once. A win earns 3 points, a draw earns 1 point to each team and a loss earns 0. At the end, the total of the points of all eight teams is 76.
The number of matches that ended in a draw is ______.
solution:
Number of matches $=\binom82=28$.
A decided match gives 3 points in all; a drawn match gives 2. With $D$ draws: $3(28-D)+2D=84-D=76$ ⇒ $D=$ 8.
Trap: with 2 points for a win the total would be fixed (56) and tell nothing.
verify:
from math import comb
M = comb(8, 2)
cands = [D for D in range(M + 1) if 3 * (M - D) + 2 * D == 76]
assert len(cands) == 1
ans = cands[0]

subtopic: weighing to find a heavier coin
q: There are 9 identical-looking coins; exactly one of them is slightly heavier than the others, which all weigh the same. Using only a two-pan balance (no weights), what is the minimum number of weighings that guarantees finding the heavier coin?
solution:
Each weighing has three outcomes (left heavy, right heavy, balance), so it can cut the suspects to one-third.
Weigh 3 vs 3: the heavy coin is in the heavier group, or in the 3 left out if balanced. Then weigh 1 vs 1 from that group of 3.
$3^2=9$ ⇒ 2 weighings suffice, and 1 weighing (3 outcomes) cannot separate 9 cases.
verify:
OPTS = ["2", "3", "4", "8"]
def can(n, w):          # can w weighings always find one heavy coin among n?
    if n <= 1: return True
    if w == 0: return False
    for k in range(1, n // 2 + 1):     # k vs k
        if can(k, w - 1) and can(n - 2 * k, w - 1):
            return True
    return False
ans = min(w for w in range(10) if can(9, w))

q:
A set of identical-looking coins contains exactly one coin that is heavier than the rest. With a two-pan balance and no weights, the heavier coin can always be identified in at most 4 weighings.
The largest number of coins for which this is possible is ______.
solution:
Each weighing has 3 outcomes, so $w$ weighings can distinguish at most $3^w$ possibilities.
Splitting into three equal groups each time achieves this bound: $3^4=$ 81.
Trap: $2^4=16$ ignores the "balanced" outcome.

q:
Five friends must cross a river using one boat. The boat can carry at most two persons at a time, and at least one person must be in the boat for it to cross.
What is the minimum number of crossings (one-way trips) needed to get all five to the other bank?
solution:
Each forward trip carries at most 2, and every forward trip except the last must be followed by a return trip carrying at least 1 back.
Net gain per forward–return pair is at most 1 person, and the last trip takes 2: after $k$ pairs, $k$ have crossed, then the last trip takes 2 ⇒ $k=3$.
Total = 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 (in general $2n-3$).
Trap: 5 ignores the return trips.

q:
You have a 3-litre jug, a 5-litre jug (neither has markings) and an unlimited water tap. One step is any one of: filling a jug completely from the tap, emptying a jug completely, or pouring from one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full.
Starting with both jugs empty, what is the minimum number of steps needed so that one of the jugs contains exactly 4 litres?
solution:
Fill 5 → (0, 5); pour into 3 → (3, 2); empty 3 → (0, 2); pour 5 into 3 → (2, 0); fill 5 → (2, 5); pour into 3 until full → (3, 4).
That is 6 steps (jug amounts written as (3-L, 5-L)).
Starting by filling the 3-litre jug needs 8 steps; a search of all states confirms no route with 5 or fewer.

q:
At a meeting, every person shook hands exactly once with every other person. A total of 66 handshakes took place.
How many persons attended the meeting?
solution:
$n$ persons give $\binom n2=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ handshakes.
$n(n-1)=132=12\times11$ ⇒ $n=$ 12.
Trap: 33 halves 66 once more; 11 is the other factor.
verify:
OPTS = ["11", "12", "13", "33"]
from itertools import combinations
cands = [n for n in range(2, 60) if len(list(combinations(range(n), 2))) == 66]
assert len(cands) == 1
ans = cands[0]

q:
Amit, Bala and Chirag come from three different cities — Delhi, Pune and Kochi — and each plays a different game — cricket, chess and tennis.
• Amit is not from Delhi and does not play chess.
• The person from Pune plays tennis.
• Bala plays cricket.
• Chirag is from Kochi.
Which game does the person from Delhi play?
solution:
Chirag is from Kochi and Amit is not from Delhi ⇒ Amit is from Pune ⇒ Amit plays tennis.
So Bala is from Delhi, and Bala plays cricket (Chirag plays chess).
Delhi: cricket.

q:
Four friends P, Q, R and S each own a different pet — cat, dog, fish, parrot — and each comes from a different city — Agra, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi.
• The dog owner is from Delhi.
• Q owns neither the cat nor the dog.
• S owns the cat and is not from Agra.
• The fish owner is from Agra, and the parrot owner is from Chennai.
• P is not from Delhi, and Q is not from Chennai.
Which pet does Q own, and which city is Q from?
solution:
The dog owner is not Q (given) or S (cat), and not P (P is not from Delhi) ⇒ R owns the dog and is from Delhi.
P and Q own the fish and the parrot. Fish ↔ Agra and parrot ↔ Chennai; Q is not from Chennai ⇒ Q owns the fish and is from Agra.
Then P: parrot, Chennai; S: cat, Bhopal.
verify:

from itertools import permutations
res = []
for pp in permutations(['cat', 'dog', 'fish', 'parrot']):
    pet = dict(zip('PQRS', pp)); byp = {v: k for k, v in pet.items()}
    for cc in permutations(['Agra', 'Bhopal', 'Chennai', 'Delhi']):
        city = dict(zip('PQRS', cc))
        if city[byp['dog']] != 'Delhi' or pet['Q'] in ('cat', 'dog') or pet['S'] != 'cat' or city['S'] == 'Agra': continue
        if city[byp['fish']] != 'Agra' or city[byp['parrot']] != 'Chennai' or city['P'] == 'Delhi' or city['Q'] == 'Chennai': continue
        res.append(f"{pet['Q'].capitalize()}, {city['Q']}")
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res[0])]

q:
Each cell of the 4 × 4 grid below is to be filled with one of the letters P, Q, R, S so that every row, every column and each of the four 2 × 2 corner blocks (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) contains all four letters.
?S
RP
PR
SQ
Which letter goes in the cell marked "?"
solution:
Row 2 is R _ P _: it needs Q and S in columns 2 and 4. Column 4 already has S (row 1) ⇒ row 2, column 4 = Q and row 2, column 2 = S.
The top-left block now has R and S, so row 1, columns 1–2 hold P and Q.
Column 2 already has P (row 3) ⇒ "?" = Q.

q:
In the 4 × 4 array below, each cell of the first three rows contains either a cross (X) or a number. Each number equals the count of its immediately neighbouring cells (left, right, up, down and the four diagonals) that do not contain a cross. The last row contains no crosses; its four cells are to be filled with numbers by the same rule.
X342
35X3
X66X
The sum of the four numbers in the last row is
solution:
Only row 3 (X _ _ X) and row 4 itself touch the last row.
Row 4, col 1: neighbours (3,1) X, (3,2), (4,2) ⇒ 2.
Col 2: (3,1) X, (3,2), (3,3), (4,1), (4,3) ⇒ 4.
Col 3: (3,2), (3,3), (3,4) X, (4,2), (4,4) ⇒ 4.
Col 4: (3,3), (3,4) X, (4,3) ⇒ 2.
Sum = 2 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 12.
Trap: corner cells have only 3 neighbours, edge cells 5.

q:
The nine numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are placed in a 3 × 3 grid, one in each cell, so that the three numbers in every row, every column and both main diagonals add up to the same total.
Which number must be in the centre cell?
solution:
Sum of all nine numbers = 54, so each row adds to 54/3 = 18.
The four lines through the centre (middle row, middle column, two diagonals) together cover every cell once and the centre four times: $4\times18=54+3c$ ⇒ $c=$ 6.
Trap: 18 is the line total, not the centre.
verify:
OPTS = ["5", "6", "7", "18"]
from itertools import permutations
centres = set()
for p in permutations(range(2, 11)):
    if p[0] + p[1] + p[2] != 18: continue
    g = [p[0:3], p[3:6], p[6:9]]
    lines = [sum(r) for r in g] + [sum(g[r][c] for r in range(3)) for c in range(3)] + [g[0][0] + g[1][1] + g[2][2], g[0][2] + g[1][1] + g[2][0]]
    if len(set(lines)) == 1:
        centres.add(g[1][1])
assert len(centres) == 1
ans = centres.pop()

q:
A pen went missing, and exactly one of A, B, C and D took it.
A: "I did not take it."
B: "D took it."
C: "B took it."
D: "I did not take it."
If exactly one of the four is lying, who took the pen?
solution:
B and C name different people, so at least one of them lies; hence exactly one of them lies and A, D are truthful ⇒ neither A nor D took it.
If C took it, both B and C lie ✗. So B took it: B lies, the rest are true ✓.
verify:
OPTS = ["B", "A", "C", "D"]
res = [X for X in 'ABCD' if [X != 'A', X == 'D', X == 'B', X != 'D'].count(False) == 1]
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res[0])]

q:
Exactly one of A, B, C and D cracked the puzzle first. They said:
A: "C did it."
B: "D did not do it."
C: "B did it."
D: "I did not do it."
Exactly two of the four statements are true. Who cracked the puzzle first?
solution:
B's and D's statements say the same thing ("D did not"), so they are both true or both false.
If both are false, D did it; then A and C are also false — zero true ✗.
So B and D are true and A, C must both be false: the culprit is not D, not C, not B ⇒ A.
Check: only B and D true ✓.
verify:
OPTS = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
res = [X for X in 'ABCD' if sum([X == 'C', X != 'D', X == 'B', X != 'D']) == 2]
assert len(res) == 1
ans = 'ABCD'[OPTS.index(res[0])]

q:
In the addition $AB+BA=CDC$, each letter stands for a different digit, $AB$ and $BA$ are two-digit numbers (so $A, B \neq 0$) and $CDC$ is a three-digit number.
The number of possible values of the two-digit number $AB$ is ______.
solution:
$AB+BA=11(A+B)$, a three-digit multiple of 11 at most $11\times17=187$.
The only three-digit palindrome among 110, 121, …, 187 is 121 ⇒ $C=1$, $D=2$, $A+B=11$.
Pairs with sum 11 avoiding the digits 1 and 2: (3, 8), (4, 7), (5, 6) and their reverses ⇒ 6 values of $AB$ ((2, 9) and (9, 2) clash with $D=2$).

q:
A knock-out tennis tournament has 50 players. Some players get a bye (advance without playing) in the first round so that the number of players entering the second round is a power of 2.
How many byes are given in the first round?
solution:
The next power of 2 above 50 is 64. Byes $=64-50=$ 14.
Check: 36 players play 18 matches; 18 winners + 14 byes = 32 = $2^5$ ✓.
Trap: 18 is the number of first-round matches.

q:
Eight players take part in a chess tournament in which every player plays every other player exactly once. A win earns 1 point, a draw earns ½ point to each player and a loss earns 0.
What is the total number of points scored by all the players together?
solution:
Every game hands out exactly 1 point in total (1 + 0 or ½ + ½).
Number of games $=\binom82=28$ ⇒ total points = 28, whatever the results.
Trap: 56 counts each game from both players' sides.
verify:
OPTS = ["28", "14", "56", "64"]
from itertools import combinations
ans = sum(1 for _ in combinations(range(8), 2)) * 1

subtopic: knights and knaves, must be true
q:
On an island every person is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
A says, "B and C are both knaves."
B says, "A is a knave."
C says, "A and B are of the same type."
Which of the following statements must be true?
options: Exactly one of A and B is a knight.
solution:
B says A is a knave: if B is a knight, A is a knave; if B is a knave, A is a knight. So exactly one of A, B is a knight ✓.
Hence A and B are of different types, so C's statement is false ⇒ C is a knave ✓.
Both (A knight, B knave, C knave) and (A knave, B knight, C knave) are consistent (A's claim is true in the first, false in the second), so neither "A is a knight" nor "B is a knave" is forced.
verify:
OPTS = ["A is a knight.", "C is a knave.", "B is a knave.", "Exactly one of A and B is a knight."]
from itertools import product
worlds = []
for a, b, c in product([True, False], repeat=3):
    if ((not b) and (not c)) == a and (not a) == b and (a == b) == c:
        worlds.append((a, b, c))
tests = [lambda w: w[0], lambda w: not w[2], lambda w: not w[1], lambda w: w[0] != w[1]]
ans = [l for l, f in zip('ABCD', tests) if all(f(w) for w in worlds)]

q:
Arun, Bina and Charu each drink a different beverage — tea, coffee, juice — and wear a different colour — red, green, blue.
• Arun does not drink tea.
• The person wearing red drinks coffee.
• Bina wears blue.
• Charu does not drink juice.
Which of the following statements must be true?
options: The person who drinks juice does not wear red.
solution:
Bina wears blue, so red is Arun or Charu.
Arun in red: Arun coffee, Charu (green) tea, Bina juice.
Charu in red: Charu coffee, Arun (green) juice, Bina tea.
In both cases coffee goes with red, so Bina (blue) never drinks coffee ✓ and the juice drinker is never in red ✓.
"Arun drinks coffee" and "Charu wears green" hold only in the first case.
verify:
OPTS = ["Bina does not drink coffee.", "Arun drinks coffee.", "The person who drinks juice does not wear red.", "Charu wears green."]
from itertools import permutations
P = ['Arun', 'Bina', 'Charu']
worlds = []
for d in permutations(['tea', 'coffee', 'juice']):
    dr = dict(zip(P, d))
    for c in permutations(['red', 'green', 'blue']):
        co = dict(zip(P, c)); byc = {v: k for k, v in co.items()}
        if dr['Arun'] != 'tea' and dr[byc['red']] == 'coffee' and co['Bina'] == 'blue' and dr['Charu'] != 'juice':
            worlds.append((dr, co))
byd = lambda dr, x: [k for k in P if dr[k] == x][0]
tests = [lambda dr, co: dr['Bina'] != 'coffee', lambda dr, co: dr['Arun'] == 'coffee',
         lambda dr, co: co[byd(dr, 'juice')] != 'red', lambda dr, co: co['Charu'] == 'green']
ans = [l for l, f in zip('ABCD', tests) if all(f(*w) for w in worlds)]

q:
A drawer contains 6 red, 8 blue and 10 black socks, all mixed up. Socks are taken out one at a time in the dark.
What is the minimum number of socks that must be taken out to be sure of having at least two black socks?
solution:
Worst case: all 6 red and all 8 blue come out first, and then one black: 15 socks with only one black.
The next sock must be black ⇒ 16.
Trap: 4 is the answer for "two socks of the same colour".
verify:
